children: By Bruce Horovitz
For most of the past 50 years, I've lived away from my Rust Belt hometown. Now — at 73 — I've retired here.
What was I thinking?
My hometown is Cleveland, where the weather is rocky, the crime high and the image sketchy.

But put that aside. It's also where many of my best friends and relatives still live. It's where fond memories of my youth intermix with new possibilities for our future. And it's where we just retired to the enchanting village of Chagrin Falls, a rustic retreat just a stone's throw south of city life, where we're more likely to spot a wandering deer in the road than a pothole.

It wasn't, however, the easiest decision. My wife, Evelyne, and I had to think hard about the arguments for and against retiring to the place I was from. Now that we've done it, and I've talked to retirement experts about the pros and cons, I've come up with a list of reasons why going home again is worth considering — and how to do it right.
The pleasures of family and friends

I spent way too much of my life running away from my friends and family. it's hard to explain why, but I think it had more to do with a discomfort I had with myself, not with them. Even at age 18, while most of my good buddies were applying to colleges in Ohio, I darted off to Colorado.

Later, as we began our careers, most of my friends settled in the Cleveland suburbs. But I, in my search for meaning, ended up hopping around California and the Washington, D.C., area. I have no complaints about any of those places, but I never found that cosmic meaning of life.

I now realize that is because it was all right here in Ohio — with my sister and cousins and best friends. Old relationships are surprisingly easy to revive when you're back in town because of all the history you share. Sure, some of the old gang now use walking sticks while others wince with arthritic knees, but we're still out there enjoying Saturday morning hikes together.

What's more, what I thought was confining when I was 18 has now become oddly comfortable and comforting at 73; the pace that was once stifling and slow now feels just right. "Community, friends, and family — all of those sweet, comfortable social connections are what juice your life as you age," says Kerry Hannon, a retirement expert and author in Washington, D.C.
This place is cheap
If retiring home means you're leaving the East Coast or the West Coast, there is a good chance you'll save a boatload.

For instance, the cost of living here in Cleveland ranks 7% below the national average. That is bolstered by the cheap cost of housing, which ranks 21% below the national average, according to the Council for Community and Economic Research. We sold our home in Northern Virginia and bought an even nicer home here in Northern Ohio, yet were able to bank nearly one-quarter of the proceeds after the sale.

Still, cautions David Conti, a retirement coach in Hampton Falls, N.H., retirees shouldn't move just for financial reasons. "Focus on family, familiarity, friends and your own future," he says. "Don't make it about the money."
Cities change

Cleveland got ridiculously hip. Maybe your hometown did, too? Much has changed for the better in the Rust Belt, and many of the cities don't look and feel anything like they did in the bad old days of the late 1970s and early 1980s.
Case in point: When visitors come, Evelyne and I take them to the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame, where you can hear people speaking so many languages you would swear you're in the Louvre Museum.
The weather factor
Weather matters — but perhaps not how you think. Most discussions among retirees involve weather, and the sunnier the better.

But at least for us, being able to play golf 24/7 wasn't much of a draw. My wife is from Bern, Switzerland, whose weather is oddly similar to Cleveland's. Seasons — even wet ones — are both familiar and an important piece of who we are.

When it comes to weather, says Hannon, it's climate change you should pay attention to. For example, Florida, Arizona and Palm Springs, Calif. — all classic retirement havens — can bite you with the soaring cost of electricity to keep you cool. As for coastal locations, the rising cost of homeowners insurance can pack a wallop, she warns.
You can't just re-create the past

Retiring home doesn't mean settling into the exact old places and old habits; you want the best of both the old and the new. That is one reason I didn't want to move back into my old Shaker Heights stamping ground, but instead to a totally different place. Our condo is within walking distance from a bustling town. And there is a woodsy path less than 100 yards from our front door where we can escape with our dog for miles of seasonal hikes.
We also are eager to make new friends and expand our interests. "We all need new — younger — friends to help keep us vibrant," says Conti.

Among other things, we signed up as volunteers at the local live theater and documentary film festival. I'm volunteering weekly at a local nonprofit that serves underprivileged youth from Cleveland's urban core. And I started writing a column for a local publication.
Here for the good — and bad

Those dreadful days of having to quickly hop on an airplane to rush home to visit an ailing relative — or attend a funeral — are in the rearview mirror. Now, I'm right here to be part of it all. Likewise, if I need an unexpected assist from a sibling or old friend, I don't have to seek long-distance help over the telephone.

These support networks, for both practical and emotional needs, form a bedrock for longer-term well-being, says Pauline Johnson-Zielonka, a retirement-planning consultant in Seal Beach, Calif. "We underestimate the need for support networks until we need them," she says.
It feels like home

After decades of living on both coasts, coming home to the familiarity of the Midwestern streets I drove, the trails I walked, and even the bakery that still sells the same chocolate chip cookies my mom would bring home as a family treat is emotionally uplifting even half a century later.

There is strong evidence that nostalgia can be good for psychological health as we age, "especially when it reconnects us with people, meaning, and a sense of continuity," says Chip Conley, founder of the Modern Elder Academy, a retreat center in Santa Fe, N.M., that helps people with aging issues.

Moving back home meant I didn't have to uproot and learn the idiosyncrasies of an entirely new community. After 35 years of living just outside Washington, D.C., I never once rooted for a D.C. sports team, but I kept my allegiance to Cleveland's often-frustrating Guardians, Cavaliers and Browns. Now, instead of watching them alone on TV, I can cheer them on in person with a lifelong friend by my side.

I have returned to the joy of familiarity — almost like finding that long-missing pair of comfy slippers that somehow got misplaced. I found them right where I left them in my hometown. Now that I've retired here and put them back on, they feel just right.
